section.title: Trust in the LORD
section.sectionRationale: The third discourse gathers a string of connected appeals around one center, verses 5 to 8, trust in the LORD with all your heart. Around that center the father urges loving devotion, honors God with wealth, welcomes His discipline, praises wisdom's cosmic worth, promises safety, and closes with practical love of neighbor and the LORD's opposition to the proud.
section.thesis: A wise life is not built on self reliant understanding but on whole hearted trust in the LORD, a trust that shapes worship, welcomes discipline, prizes wisdom above riches, and works itself out in concrete kindness toward others.
section.frameNote: Six movements: bind loving devotion and faithfulness to yourself, verses 1 to 4; trust in the LORD, the chapter's center, verses 5 to 8; honor the LORD with wealth and welcome His discipline, verses 9 to 12; the surpassing worth of wisdom, verses 13 to 20; safety for the one who keeps sound judgment, verses 21 to 26; and practical love of neighbor closing with the LORD's grace to the humble, verses 27 to 35.

verses.text: My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments;
for they will add length to your days, years and peace to your life.
Never let {{chesed|loving devotion}} or faithfulness leave you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart.
Then you will find favor and high regard in the sight of God and man.
Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding;
in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight.
Be not wise in your own eyes; {{yirah|fear}} the LORD and turn away from evil.
This will bring healing to your body and refreshment to your bones.

units.label: Honor the LORD, welcome His discipline
units.note: wealth and correction both belong to Him

verses.text: Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your harvest;
then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will overflow with new wine.
My son, do not reject the {{musar|discipline}} of the LORD, and do not loathe His rebuke;
for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights.
Blessed is the man who finds {{chokmah|wisdom}}, the man who acquires understanding,
for she is more profitable than silver, and her gain is better than fine gold.
She is more precious than rubies; nothing you desire compares with her.
Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor.
All her ways are pleasant, and all her paths are peaceful.
She is a tree of life to those who embrace her, and those who lay hold of her are blessed.
The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding.
By His knowledge the watery depths were broken open, and the clouds dripped with dew.

units.label: Safety for the one who keeps sound judgment

verses.text: My son, do not lose sight of this: Preserve sound judgment and discernment.
They will be life to your soul and adornment to your neck.
Then you will go on your way in safety, and your foot will not stumble.
When you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you rest, your sleep will be sweet.
Do not fear sudden danger or the ruin that overtakes the wicked,
for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from the snare.

units.label: Love your neighbor, and the LORD's grace to the humble

verses.text: Do not withhold good from the deserving when it is within your power to act.
Do not tell your neighbor, "Come back tomorrow and I will provide," when you already have the means.
Do not devise evil against your neighbor, for he trustfully dwells beside you.
Do not accuse a man without cause, when he has done you no harm.
Do not envy a violent man or choose any of his ways;
for the LORD detests the perverse, but He is a friend to the upright.
The curse of the LORD is on the house of the wicked, but He blesses the home of the righteous.
He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble.
The wise will inherit honor, but fools are held up to shame.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, a rich word covering love, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and loyalty to a covenant. It is most often used of God's covenant love, but here the son is told to bind it around his own neck, letting God's covenant love shape his own character toward others.

yirah.gloss: The fear of the LORD, reverent trust that turns away from evil. Paired here with not being wise in your own eyes, it marks humility before God as the opposite of self reliant understanding.

musar.gloss: Discipline or correction. Verses 11 to 12 reframe discipline as evidence of fatherly love rather than divine hostility, a text the New Testament quotes directly in Hebrews 12:5-6 to comfort believers under hardship.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, praised here as more valuable than silver, gold, or rubies, and as the very instrument by which the LORD founded the earth and the heavens, verses 19 to 20. She is pictured as a tree of life to those who embrace her.

basic.context: This chapter strings together some of the most beloved lines in Proverbs, do not lean on your own understanding, honor the LORD with your wealth, do not despise His discipline, wisdom is more precious than rubies, and He gives grace to the humble. Read as a whole, it teaches that a life built on trusting God, not on self sufficient cleverness, is the true path to safety, blessing, and a good name.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter moves like a string of pearls, each section connected to whole hearted trust in God. Verses 5 to 8 are its literal and thematic center: trust, not self reliant understanding, is the operating principle beneath worship, discipline, wisdom, safety, and neighbor love alike. None of this is magic; it describes the normal shape of a God trusting life, not a formula that removes all hardship, as verses 11 to 12 make explicit by assuming that God's own children will be disciplined, sometimes painfully.
basic.originalLanguages: Chesed, loving devotion, is the rich covenant word for God's own faithful love, here commanded as a trait to bind around one's own neck. Musar, discipline, in verses 11 to 12 is reframed as proof of fatherly love, a connection so important the author of Hebrews quotes it directly. And chokmah, wisdom, is praised as more valuable than any treasure and as the very means by which the LORD founded the world, verses 19 to 20.
basic.typology: Wisdom as a tree of life, verse 18, and as the one through whom the world was founded, verses 19 to 20, anticipates the New Testament's description of Christ as the one through whom and for whom all things were created, Colossians 1:16, and as the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24. The discipline of a loving father, verses 11 to 12, points to God's fatherly discipline of every child He receives, Hebrews 12:5 to 6.
basic.christ: This chapter's center, trust in the LORD rather than your own understanding, finds its deepest ground in Christ, who trusted the Father perfectly, even to the point of death, and who is Himself the wisdom by which the world was made, Colossians 1:16 to 17, 1 Corinthians 1:24. The discipline commended in verses 11 to 12 is quoted in Hebrews 12:5 to 6 as proof that God treats believers as true sons, disciplined because of, not despite, His love shown fully at the cross.
basic.god: God is the one worth trusting completely, the one who deserves the firstfruits of all we have, the Father who disciplines those He loves, and the giver of a wisdom so vast that the earth and heavens themselves rest on it. He is also humble toward the humble, giving grace to them while opposing the proud, a truth quoted twice in the New Testament, James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 12:5 to 6 quotes verses 11 to 12 directly on the discipline of a loving Father. James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 quote verse 34 on grace for the humble. Colossians 1:16 to 17 presents Christ as the one through whom all things were created, echoing wisdom's role in verses 19 to 20. 1 Corinthians 1:24 calls Christ the wisdom of God.
basic.oneStory: Trust in the LORD, not self reliant understanding, is the thread running through this whole chapter, worship, discipline, wisdom, safety, and neighbor love all flow from it. That same trust finds its fullest object in Christ, the wisdom by whom the world was made and the Son who trusted His Father even to the cross, so that all who trust in Him receive both fatherly discipline and unearned grace.

context.literary:
Proverbs 3 is built from three addresses that each open with the same call, "My son," in verses 1, 11 and 21. Inside that frame the chapter reads as a series of short lessons, each ending on a promise or a warning. Verses 1 to 12 set two commands side by side, keep the teaching and trust the LORD, and verses 21 to 35 return to the teaching and turn it toward the neighbor. Between them stands the hymn to wisdom, verses 13 to 20, introduced by the only beatitude in the chapter, "Blessed is the man," and closed by a sudden widening of the lens from the young man's career to the founding of the cosmos.

Notice the pairs of body language that run through the chapter. In verse 3 faithfulness is bound "around your neck," and in verse 22 sound judgment returns as "adornment to your neck," so the chapter's first movement and fourth movement rhyme. Verse 8 promises health to the body and bones, verse 22 life to the soul. The word "all" does heavy lifting: "all your heart," "all your ways," "all your harvest," "all her ways," "all her paths." Nothing is left outside the claim.

The center is not decoration. Verses 5 to 8 give four lines, two commands and two promises, and they turn on a pair of opposites, the heart that trusts and the understanding that leans on itself. Everything before it, the teaching written on the heart, prepares for that trust, and everything after it, worship, discipline, wisdom's worth, safety and justice toward neighbors, is trust lived out. The closing verses sharpen the choice with a run of contrasts: perverse against upright, cursed against blessed, mockers against the humble, honor against shame.

Within the book, chapter 3 is the third of the father's lectures in the opening collection, Proverbs 1 to 9, which frames the sayings of the later chapters. Its job is to supply the reason to listen before the sentence-length proverbs begin.
context.historical:
The father speaks as an Israelite householder, and the chapter is full of his world. Verse 9 assumes a farming economy in which the first portion of the crop was set apart for the LORD, as the law required in Exodus 23:19 and Deuteronomy 26:1-11. The barns and wine vats of verse 10 are the visible shape of the covenant blessing promised for obedience, "The LORD will decree a blessing on your barns," Deuteronomy 28:8. The first hearers would have caught that echo at once. Honoring God with the firstfruits meant acting as though the harvest was a gift before it was even gathered in.

The promise of undisturbed sleep and of a foot that will not stumble, verses 23 to 24, has the same background. The covenant blessings of Leviticus 26:6 include lying down "with nothing to fear," and ordinary life in a country of bandits, wild animals, raiding armies and sudden crop failure gave the promise real weight. "Sudden danger," verse 25, names the kind of terror that Proverbs 1:26-27 had already described as the harvest of ignoring wisdom, and Proverbs 1:33 promised security to the one who listens.

Verses 27 to 29 reflect village life. A man with grain or silver in his house could easily say "come back tomorrow." Hired workers lived day to day, which is why the law says wages are not to be held back until morning, Leviticus 19:13. A neighbor in a small community "trustfully dwells beside you," sleeping within earshot, with no police or locks to rely on, and so was easy to harm.

The attribution of the book to Solomon, Proverbs 1:1, places the collection in the early monarchy, when the court was known for its learning. The language of a father instructing his son fits both the home and the training of young officials. Whatever its setting, the instruction assumes the young man will soon hold property, give testimony and be tempted to follow men who seem to prosper by force.
context.canonical:
Few chapters of Proverbs are quoted as often as this one. Verses 11 and 12 reappear in Hebrews 12:5-6, which introduces them as an exhortation "that addresses you as sons." Hebrews cites the Greek translation, and the BSB footnotes record that it reads "and do not lose heart when He rebukes" and "He chastises every son He receives." The risen Christ alludes to the same teaching when He says, "Those I love, I rebuke and discipline," Revelation 3:19. Verse 34, in the Greek form "The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble," is quoted by James 4:6 and by Peter, 1 Peter 5:5.

Other New Testament writers pick up lines without announcing them. Paul's warning against pride and conceit, Romans 12:16, and his instruction to consider "what is right in the eyes of everybody," Romans 12:17, recall verses 7 and 4. Luke's note that Jesus "grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man," Luke 2:52, almost repeats verse 4.

The chapter also looks back. The tablet of the heart in verse 3 draws on the commands of Deuteronomy 6:6-9, to keep God's words on the heart, bind them on the hand and write them on the doorposts, and it looks ahead to the promise of the new covenant, "inscribe it on their hearts," Jeremiah 31:33. The tree of life in verse 18 sends a reader back to Genesis 2:9 and 3:22-24 and forward to Revelation 2:7 and 22:2.

Wisdom's work in creation, verses 19 to 20, is developed in Proverbs 8:22-31, in Psalm 104:24 and in Jeremiah 10:12. The New Testament carries the thought to its destination in the Son through whom the world was made, Colossians 1:16 and John 1:3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The father wants his son to see that trust is a way of knowing, not only a feeling. When he says "in all your ways acknowledge Him," he asks the young man to bring God into decisions about money, friendships, work and justice, not only into the temple. He does not set trust against thinking. He sets it against a particular kind of thinking, the kind that treats its own insight as the last court of appeal.

He also wants the son to expect to be corrected. A young man who has just been told to trust the LORD might assume that trust means a smooth road. By verse 11 the father says plainly that the LORD will discipline, and he gives the reason in the same breath. The correction comes from a Father who delights in the son. The aim is to keep a good boy from reading hardship as abandonment.

The last third of the chapter pushes the claim out into daily conduct. The son who trusts the LORD does not delay paying a worker, does not plot against a neighbor who sleeps trustfully nearby, does not quarrel without cause and does not envy the violent. The chapter closes with God's verdict on two kinds of life, the perverse He detests and the upright He befriends. The son is meant to leave the lesson knowing which household he wants to belong to.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The verbs are mostly commands: do not forget, bind, trust, acknowledge, honor, do not reject, do not withhold, do not devise evil. The promises that follow them are statements about how life usually goes under God's moral order, so a reader should not turn each one into a contract. A person who trusts and still faces illness, poverty or a long road has not failed the proverb, because the same chapter expects discipline and danger, verses 11 and 25.

Application starts by keeping command and promise in their own places. The commands bind believers today, and the New Testament repeats them, Romans 12:17 and Hebrews 12:5-6. The promises are the Father's encouragement, not a payment schedule. Verses 9 and 10 are the clearest test. Honoring the LORD with the firstfruits is commanded, and full barns are the ordinary fruit of a life lived in His care. Giving in order to get misses the point, since firstfruits are given before the harvest is known. Paul's teaching in 2 Corinthians 9:6-8 keeps the same balance, calling for cheerful giving and promising God's sufficiency, not a guaranteed return.

debates.question: Does verse 9, honoring the LORD with wealth for full barns in return, teach a guaranteed prosperity?

views.label: A description of God's normal, generous pattern
views.case: Verse 10 states a real, general connection between honoring God with resources and material blessing, consistent with the broader wisdom tradition that generosity tends toward flourishing.

views.label: A general proverb, not an unconditional formula
views.case: Proverbs elsewhere shows the righteous suffering and the wicked prospering, Proverbs 13:23, Ecclesiastes 7:15, so this verse describes the ordinary tendency of honoring God with resources, not a mechanical transaction that guarantees wealth to every giver.

debates.bearing: Read within the whole of Proverbs and Scripture, verse 9 to 10 commends generous, God honoring stewardship as wise and normally fruitful, without turning giving into a guaranteed exchange for riches, a distortion the prosperity gospel makes of texts like this one.

debates.question: How should verses 11 to 12 shape a Christian's view of hardship?

views.label: Hardship as evidence of God's fatherly love
views.case: Hebrews 12:5 to 6 quotes this passage to comfort suffering believers, arguing that discipline itself is proof of sonship, not divine rejection.

views.label: A warning against resenting or despising correction
views.case: The command is as much about the son's response, do not reject, do not loathe, as about the fact of discipline itself, aiming at humble acceptance rather than bitterness or self pity.

debates.bearing: Both readings work together, the passage teaches that God's discipline is loving, and it calls for a humble, trusting response rather than resentment, exactly the pastoral use Hebrews makes of it.

debates.question: Why does Hebrews 12:6 word the end of verse 12 differently from the Hebrew text?

views.label: The Greek translator worked from a different Hebrew text
views.case: Hebrews quotes the Greek version, which reads that the Lord 'chastises every son He receives,' where the Hebrew says a father corrects 'the son in whom he delights.' Some think the translator had a slightly different wording before him.

views.label: The Greek translator was interpreting, not copying
views.case: Others think the change is a free rendering that spells out the idea of sonship and the sharpness of correction, since the Hebrew verb for corrects and the thought of a delighted father already imply both.

debates.bearing: Whichever explanation is right, the New Testament writer uses the line as Scripture and keeps its meaning intact. Discipline falls on every son and comes from delight, so the passage can be trusted for what it says about God's character even when its wording passes through a translation.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter turns on a handful of Hebrew words that the English flattens. The first is batach, the verb for trust in verse 5. It has the sense of resting one's weight on something and feeling secure. The same root appears in verse 29, where the neighbor "trustfully dwells" beside you, and the echo is deliberate. The man who is told to put all his security in the LORD is also told not to betray the security another man has placed in him. The verb that follows, "lean not," is sha'an, to rest on a support as a man rests on a staff, and the support named is the speaker's own binah, understanding. The line does not condemn understanding. It refuses to let understanding hold the weight that belongs to the LORD.

Verse 6 asks the son to "acknowledge" the LORD. The Hebrew verb is yada, to know, so the instruction is to know Him in all one's ways, to treat Him as a familiar party to every decision. The promise that He will "make your paths straight" uses yashar, the root for level and upright. The moral and the physical meanings overlap, so a straight path is both a safe one and a right one. The BSB footnote to verse 8 notes that the word rendered "body" is literally "navel," and that "healing" may also be read as "medicine," which gives the verse a bodily, almost physical picture of what fear and humility do for a person.

In verse 9 "honor" is kabbed, from the root of kavod, which has to do with weight or glory. To honor the LORD with wealth is to give Him the weight in one's accounting. "Firstfruits" translates reshit, the beginning or first, a word that also opens Genesis 1:1 and names wisdom's own place in Proverbs 8:22. The first of the harvest belongs to the LORD because He is first.

In verse 12 the Hebrew says a father corrects the son "in whom he delights." That verb of delight expresses the tender motive behind correction. The Greek translation, which Hebrews follows, reads instead that He "chastises every son He receives," a harder word that makes the point that sonship and chastening travel together.

Finally, verses 4 and 22 and 34 are tied by the word chen, grace or favor. The son who binds in faithfulness will find chen in the sight of God and man, verse 4. Wisdom becomes chen about his neck, verse 22, and the LORD gives chen to the humble, verse 34. The Hebrew of verse 32 adds that the LORD's sod, His intimate counsel, belongs to the upright, which the BSB renders "a friend," compare Psalm 25:14, where the LORD "confides in those who fear Him." Grace and friendship are the reward the chapter offers.

typology.type: Wisdom as the tree of life, Proverbs 3:18
typology.fulfillment: The tree of life stood in Eden and was guarded after the fall, Genesis 3:22-24. Proverbs says wisdom is a tree of life for those who embrace her, and later proverbs apply the picture to the fruit of the righteous, Proverbs 11:30, to fulfilled hope, Proverbs 13:12, and to a soothing tongue, Proverbs 15:4. The New Testament says Christ was hung on a tree, Acts 5:30 and 1 Peter 2:24, and promises the tree of life to the overcomer, Revelation 2:7, and its leaves for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. The picture is poetic in Proverbs, so the link is by theme and not by prediction. The type falls short because wisdom gives life only as a way to live; Christ gives it as a gift won by His death.

typology.type: Wisdom as the LORD's instrument in making the world, Proverbs 3:19-20
typology.fulfillment: Wisdom, understanding and knowledge appear here as the tools of creation, and the same three words describe the skill God gave Bezalel to build the tabernacle, Exodus 31:3, as though the sanctuary were a small copy of the world. The New Testament says the world was made through the Son, John 1:3, Colossians 1:16-17 and Hebrews 1:2, and calls Him the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, Colossians 2:3. Proverbs personifies wisdom without saying she is a person of the Godhead, so Christian readers read the link through the later revelation. The type falls short because wisdom here is an attribute of God, while the Son is a Person who became flesh.

typology.type: The firstfruits given to the LORD, Proverbs 3:9
typology.fulfillment: The first part of the harvest was set apart as God's own and acted as a pledge that the whole belonged to Him, Deuteronomy 26:1-11. Paul uses the same word for Christ, who has been raised as 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and for believers who have the Spirit as the firstfruits of what is coming, Romans 8:23. The first sheaf promised the rest of the harvest. In Christ's resurrection, the first fruit is the guarantee that a whole harvest of the dead will follow, 1 Corinthians 15:23. The pattern falls short in that Israel's firstfruits were something offered up by the worshipper, while Christ is both the offering and the One raised.

typology.type: The law written on the tablet of the heart, Proverbs 3:3
typology.fulfillment: The son is told to write loving devotion and faithfulness on the tablet of his heart, a command he cannot fully carry out. The prophets say God Himself will do what the proverb commands, 'I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:33, and Ezekiel promises a new heart and a new spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27. Paul tells the Corinthians they are 'a letter from Christ,' written 'not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3. The proverb sets the duty, and the new covenant supplies the power. The type falls short because the proverb leaves the writing to the student, which is the very thing that fails without the Spirit.

study.christ:
Start with the chapter's quietest echo, Luke 2:52. The only summary Luke gives of Jesus' boyhood and young manhood is that He "grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man." That is Proverbs 3:4 lived out, favor in the sight of both God and man, and it is set beside wisdom. In Jesus the father's hope for a son is met. He keeps the teaching, He is trusted by God and respected by those who know Him, and He does it without losing anything of His own authority. The young man of Proverbs 3 is told to bind faithfulness around his neck. Jesus is faithfulness in person.

The heart of the chapter, trust in the LORD rather than your own understanding, is tested in Him at its hardest. In Gethsemane He asked that the cup pass and then said, "not as I will, but as You will," Matthew 26:39. On the cross He was mocked with the very words of trust, "He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him," Matthew 27:43. Hebrews says He "learned obedience from what He suffered," Hebrews 5:8, and holds Him up as the one who endured the cross for the joy set before Him, Hebrews 12:2. The father's command to lean not on one's own understanding is met by a Son who leaned wholly on the Father, even when no help could be seen.

Then there is the discipline of verses 11 and 12. Hebrews quotes the lines to explain suffering, and the very next paragraph points to Jesus, who endured opposition from sinners, Hebrews 12:3. The Son was not disciplined for sin, but He went through suffering that taught obedience, and He now stands as the pioneer of all who are brought to glory as sons, Hebrews 2:10. And it is the risen Christ who says to the church at Laodicea, "Those I love, I rebuke and discipline. Therefore be earnest and repent," Revelation 3:19, so the Lord speaks the proverb as His own.

The hymn to wisdom, verses 13 to 20, is where the New Testament makes its boldest move. Paul says Christ is "the wisdom of God," 1 Corinthians 1:24, that He has "become to us wisdom from God," 1 Corinthians 1:30, and that in Him are hidden "all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge," Colossians 2:3. That last phrase picks up the language of verses 14 and 15, wisdom better than silver and gold, nothing you desire compares with her. And the tree of life that wisdom is to those who hold her is, in the end, bound up with the cross, where Christ hung "on a tree," 1 Peter 2:24.

A word of care. Proverbs 3 does not say that wisdom is the Son. It speaks of an attribute and a way of life, and it would be a mistake to read every line as a coded reference to Jesus. The New Testament's own use, not clever allegory, justifies the links. What the chapter supplies is the pattern of a life of trust, and Christ is the one in whom that pattern is finally lived without failure and then given to His people.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He is worth trusting with the whole of a person's life. The command is not "trust Me about the spiritual things." It is "trust in the LORD with all your heart" and "in all your ways acknowledge Him," verses 5 and 6. The ground for such a claim is given in verses 19 and 20, where the same God is seen founding the earth by wisdom, establishing the heavens by understanding and breaking open the deeps by His knowledge. A God who made everything with wisdom can be trusted with one man's road.

He is a Father, and His fatherhood includes correction. Verse 12 says He disciplines the one He loves, as a father the son in whom he delights. That is a startling pairing of two words that many readers keep apart. Delight and rebuke come from the same heart. This tells us that God's fatherly purpose is character and not comfort, and that He never disciplines out of irritation or boredom. Hebrews takes the same view, saying the aim is that we share His holiness, Hebrews 12:10.

He is generous but He is not a bargain partner. The firstfruits belong to Him before the harvest is known, and the promise of full barns is His to give as He chooses. The passage shows Him as the God who gives the covenant blessing described in Deuteronomy 28:8, but the same Proverbs says elsewhere that the righteous can suffer. Both facts have to be held together, and they point to a God who is free and good, not mechanical.

He takes sides in the moral world. Verse 32 says He detests the perverse and befriends the upright. The word for friendship carries the idea of confiding, as Psalm 25:14 says, "The LORD confides in those who fear Him." Verse 33 sets His curse on the house of the wicked and His blessing on the home of the righteous, and verse 34 gives the clearest picture of His character in the chapter. He mocks the mockers, and He gives grace to the humble. The same God who stands against pride bends toward the lowly, which is why James and Peter both quote the line when they call for humility.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to come as people who need no reputation for cleverness. We bring the firstfruits, accept correction without bitterness and keep our word to a neighbor, because the God we trust sees all of it. The fear of the LORD in verse 7 is not terror. It is the stance of a child who knows who is Father and who is not.

crossReferences.note: Quotes verses 11 and 12 and calls them an exhortation addressed to sons. The writer uses the Greek form, which says the Lord chastises every son He receives, and applies it to suffering under persecution. Discipline is treated as a mark of belonging in the family, and the chapter goes on to name its fruit, a harvest of righteousness and peace, Hebrews 12:11.

The risen Lord tells the lukewarm church at Laodicea, 'Those I love, I rebuke and discipline.' The pairing of love and rebuke is the logic of Proverbs 3:12, now spoken by Christ Himself. The command that follows, to be earnest and repent, shows what the proverb meant by receiving correction without despising it.

Quotes verse 34 in its Greek form, that God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble, and uses it to explain why quarrels and worldly ambition cut a person off from God. Grace flows to those who admit they are empty, and the next verse tells them to submit to God and resist the devil, James 4:7.

Peter uses the same line to ask the young to submit to the elders and everyone to clothe themselves in humility toward one another. The picture of clothing recalls the way wisdom and faithfulness are worn about the neck in verses 3 and 22. The humble can cast their anxieties on God, 1 Peter 5:7, which is verse 5 put into practice.

The promise of a blessing on the barns is the covenant background to verse 10. Proverbs applies Israel's covenant pattern to the individual son. Deuteronomy ties the blessing to obedience, and Proverbs ties it to honoring the LORD with the firstfruits, so neither text reads as a formula for getting rich.

Forbids holding back a hired worker's wages until morning. It is the law behind verses 27 and 28, where the son is told not to say 'Come back tomorrow' when he already has the means. Proverbs turns a rule about wages into a habit of heart, doing good the moment it is possible.

Says that the LORD confides in those who fear Him and reveals His covenant to them. It helps to explain verse 32, where the upright are God's friends. The Hebrew idea behind the word is that of a confidential circle. The one who fears the LORD is let into His counsel.

Paul says all things were created through the Son and for Him, and that in Him all things hold together. This is where the New Testament lands after reading the picture of wisdom founding the earth in verses 19 and 20. The passage is not an exact quotation but the same claim brought to its personal source.

Calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God to those who are called. Paul sets this against a world that looks for wisdom in eloquence and finds the cross foolish. The father in Proverbs 3 tells his son that wisdom is better than silver, and Paul tells the church that the cross is where that wisdom is found.

The promise of the new covenant, 'I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts,' answers verse 3, where the son is told to write loving devotion on the tablet of his heart. What the proverb requires of the son, God promises to do for His people, and so the command and the gift stand side by side in Scripture.

Luke's single sentence on Jesus' growth borrows the shape of verse 4, favor in the sight of God and man. It is the one place where the Gospels say that the Son grew in wisdom. The wisdom of Proverbs 3 is lived out by the man who is, at the same time, the wisdom of God.

Paul's counsel not to be proud or conceited, and to consider what is right in the eyes of everybody, carries the stamp of verses 4 and 7. He reads Proverbs as the practical manual of the Christian community, showing that the young man's lessons have not been replaced but taken up into life in Christ.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a tree and a question of trust. In Eden the man and woman were given every tree but one, and the serpent's whole strategy was to move them from trusting God's word to relying on their own judgment of what was good, Genesis 3:5-6. Proverbs 3:5 to 7 is the reverse of that scene. The father tells his son to do the very thing Adam did not do, to trust the LORD and not his own understanding, and then he offers the son a tree of life, verse 18, the thing Adam was driven from, Genesis 3:24. Wisdom is the way back toward Eden, the first sign in the book that the damage of Genesis 3 can be mended by a way of living.

The chapter also carries Israel's story. The firstfruits, the barns and the safe sleep are the language of the covenant at Sinai and of the land God was giving. The warning against leaning on one's own understanding is also the warning of the prophets who found Israel trusting alliances and armies, and it explains why the nation went into exile despite every sign of God's care. The discipline of verses 11 and 12 is the same discipline the law described in Deuteronomy 8:5, where the Lord disciplines His people as a man disciplines his son.

All of these lines converge on Christ. He is the Son who grew in wisdom and favor, Luke 2:52, who trusted the Father to the cross, who was raised as the firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and through whom the world was made, Colossians 1:16. He bore the curse that stands against the house of the wicked and opened the way to God's friendship. What the proverb calls grace to the humble is given in Him, and the Spirit writes on hearts what the father could only tell his son to write, 2 Corinthians 3:3.

The story ends with the tree of life restored. In the new Jerusalem the tree stands by the river and its leaves are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2, and nothing accursed will be found there, Revelation 22:3. The promise to the one who overcomes, to eat from the tree of life, Revelation 2:7, is the full form of the promise to those who lay hold of wisdom in verse 18. The people who trusted the LORD with all their hearts will walk a path that is finally straight, with the God who made the heavens by wisdom dwelling among them.

sermon.title: Wisdom: How To Get It
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly through Proverbs 3:1-8 and 11-12, the heart of this chapter, unpacking what it means to trust in the LORD with all your heart and to receive His discipline as the love of a father.

quiz.q: What is the chapter's central command, stated in verses 5 to 6?

options.text: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.
options.note: This is the exact wording and thematic center of the whole chapter.

options.text: Work hard and trust your own judgment above all else.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the passage commands.

options.text: Seek wealth first, and wisdom will follow.
options.note: The chapter reverses this order, honoring God and trusting Him comes first, and material blessing is described as flowing from that, not the other way around.

options.text: Trust experts and teachers more than Scripture.
options.note: Listening to teaching matters elsewhere in Proverbs, but this passage's specific command is to trust the LORD Himself, not human experts as such.

quiz.q: How does the chapter describe God's discipline in verses 11 to 12?

options.text: As proof of fatherly love, like a father who disciplines the son he delights in.
options.note: This is quoted directly in Hebrews 12:5-6 to comfort believers under hardship.

options.text: As a sign that God has rejected the one being disciplined.
options.note: The passage explicitly says the opposite, discipline flows from love, not rejection.

options.text: As something only unbelievers experience.
options.note: The image is of a father and a beloved son, describing God's people, not those outside His family.

options.text: As a punishment with no relational meaning.
options.note: This misses the passage's emphasis on fatherly delight and love as the reason for the discipline, not bare punishment.

quiz.q: How is wisdom described in verses 13 to 20?

options.text: More precious than rubies, a tree of life, and the LORD's own instrument in founding the earth and heavens.
options.note: All three images appear directly in this section.

options.text: A minor and optional virtue.
options.note: The passage instead exalts wisdom as supremely valuable and cosmically significant.

options.text: Available only to kings and the wealthy.
options.note: The passage addresses 'my son' broadly, not a wealthy elite.

options.text: Useful mainly for financial success.
options.note: Financial gain is mentioned, verse 14, but the passage's larger claim is about wisdom's incomparable worth and cosmic role, not merely money.

quiz.q: What does verse 34 say about the LORD's dealings with the proud and the humble, and where is it quoted in the New Testament?

options.text: He mocks the mockers but gives grace to the humble, quoted in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.
options.note: This is the exact verse and its two New Testament citations.

options.text: He treats the proud and humble exactly the same.
options.note: The verse draws a sharp contrast between the two, not sameness.

options.text: He rewards pride if it produces results.
options.note: This directly contradicts the verse, which says He mocks the mockers.

options.text: It is quoted once, in Romans, on justification.
options.note: Close on the idea of a New Testament citation, but the actual quotations are in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5, on humility, not in Romans on justification.

quiz.q: How does wisdom's role in founding the earth, verses 19 to 20, point to Christ?

options.text: Christ is the one through whom and for whom all things were created, and in whom all things hold together.
options.note: Colossians 1:16-17 makes this connection directly, and 1 Corinthians 1:24 calls Christ the wisdom of God.

options.text: It shows wisdom as a purely human trait with no connection to Christ.
options.note: The passage's language of founding the earth points beyond a merely human virtue to something the New Testament applies to Christ Himself.

options.text: It teaches that Christ is less significant than divine wisdom.
options.note: The New Testament instead identifies Christ Himself as the wisdom of God, not something lesser than it.

options.text: It is a poetic image with no theological weight.
options.note: This understates how directly the New Testament builds on this very image to describe Christ's role in creation.

questions: Verse 5 calls for trust in the LORD with all your heart, not leaning on your own understanding. Where in your life right now are you leaning most heavily on your own reasoning instead of trusting God?
Verses 11 to 12 reframe discipline as evidence of a father's love. What hardship or correction are you currently tempted to resent, and how might seeing it as fatherly love change your response?
The chapter prizes wisdom above silver, gold, and rubies. If someone looked at how you spend your time and money, would they conclude that you value wisdom that highly?

Verses 27 to 31 call for concrete kindness and honesty toward neighbors, not withholding good, not delaying help you could give now. Who is someone you could bless today rather than putting off until tomorrow?
Verse 34 says God gives grace to the humble but opposes the proud. Where do you need to trade self reliant pride for humble trust in God this week?

translationNotes.note: This will bring healing renders a Hebrew phrase literally meaning to your navel, an idiom for the whole body's vitality; some translations render the second half as medicine to your bones.

The Septuagint reading, quoted in Hebrews 12:5-6, reads slightly differently, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you, and He flogs every son He receives, a wording the New Testament author follows directly.
The Septuagint reading, quoted in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5, reads the Lord opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, the exact form both New Testament letters cite.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Proverbs 3:1-35. the wording is otherwise unchanged and complete.
